content.title: A Blossoming Partnership
content.text: An original project from beginning to end That interaction with the community plays a central role in “The Beauty Project,” the culmination of a three-semester project spearheaded by KSU faculty members Nicole B. Adkins and Emily Kitchens. It consisted of a semester to devise and create the plot, a semester to write a script and experiment collaboratively, and a semester to cast and produce. All three semesters are spent on-site. Every aspect of the production originated within KSU’s Robert S. Geer Family College of the Arts, enthusiastically exported into the community by the practitioners themselves.“It is powerful to connect as a community, to talk openly about body image, beauty, and appearance culture, and to give ourselves time to be in nature,” said Adkins, a playwright who specializes in theater for young audiences. “That's what theater does best, bringing people together to collaborate.”A cast of 15 actors and five crew members, plus a troupe of dancers directed by Associate Professor of Dance Andrea Knowlton, brought to life a modern take on Lewis Carroll’s world to Smith-Gilbert Gardens. The cast features six Alices, representing a range of body types and ethnicities, a community of its own. The production begins at an arch near the gardens’ seasonal butterfly exhibit that served as the iconic looking glass. From there, the play moves to a little theater in the woods, a patch of grass between trees, the porch of the viewing pavilion in the middle of the gardens, and then to another open area in the event lawn. The play features rhyming poetry, dancing, singing, and an evolving lesson about what constitutes beauty delivered in a memorable, participatory fashion by eliminating the theatrical fourth wall; the audience plays a critical role in the production, mingling with the actors, using hearts from a deck of cards as “currency,” and pushing the narrative forward with their reactions to the performance.The dancers serve as the Jabberwock, and six Alices in evolving stages of life, from a young child to a grownup, reflect the shifting idea of beauty. The life in the garden plays a role, too, as one scene celebrates the life of Ellie, a mosquito that meets its end at the literal hands of a character, while another scene asks the difference between a wildflower and a weed.
